html:
The big picture

A robot is an automatically operated machine, controlled by a computer, that does work in place of a human; robotics is the engineering discipline of designing, building and operating such machines. The lecture gives the vocabulary to describe any robot: what it is made of (links connected by joints, ending in an end effector that does the work on a workpiece), how much it can carry (payload), how it can move (degrees of freedom, work envelope, reach) and in which coordinate systems we describe that motion. Industrial arms are classified by their joints into Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical and articulated configurations, plus specialised designs (SCARA, delta). Mobile robots are classified by how they move: wheeled (number and type of wheels decide stability and manoeuvrability), aerial and aquatic, with bio-inspired designs borrowing from animals. Each design trades workspace, precision, speed and payload against each other, and picking the right one is the recurring exam question.

What is a robot?

  • Automated (smart) machines.
  • One of the first uses of the word came from Czech writer Karel Čapek, who used it in his play "Rossum's Universal Robots", in 1920.
  • Isaac Asimov is generally given the credit for being the first person to use the term "robotics", in the 1940s.

Asimov's laws of robotics

  1. A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
  2. A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
  3. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

Robots in fiction and popular media; robots in reality

Pictures of fictional robots (C-3PO and R2-D2, the Terminator, Bender) next to real ones: an industrial welding line, a robot vacuum cleaner, a legged robot dog, an underwater drone and a quadcopter.

Robot definition

robot, a machine controlled by a computer that is used to perform jobs automatically. — Cambridge Dictionary

robot, any automatically operated machine that replaces human effort, though it may not resemble human beings in appearance or perform functions in a humanlike manner. By extension, robotics is the engineering discipline dealing with the design, construction, and operation of robots. — Britannica

Intuition: what the definitions have in common

Both definitions boil down to two ingredients: automatic operation (it runs a program, not a human hand on the controls) and doing work that would otherwise need human effort. Looks don't matter: a welding arm and a vacuum cleaner are robots, a humanoid statue isn't. A remote-controlled toy car is a borderline case: it moves, but a human makes every decision.

Applications

Example slides: modern industrial robots; exploration (a planetary rover, a deep-sea vehicle); autonomous driving / ADAS (Advanced Driver Assistance Systems), with GPS, lidar, video cameras, ultrasonic sensors, radar, odometry sensors and a central computer, each labelled with a typical cost.

  • Manufacturing: welding, assembly, metal forming, paint dispensing, part transfer, packaging
  • Logistics
  • Safety, inspection and health monitoring of machines
  • Agriculture
  • Healthcare
  • Entertainment
  • Military

Evolution of robotics research

A diagram (Garcia et al., "The evolution of robotics research", IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine, March 2007) shows research moving from industrial robots (1960s) towards mobile, walking, humanoid, underwater, field, personal, medical and service robots.

Industrial revolutions, Industry 5.0?

A timeline: Industry 1.0 (mechanisation, steam power, 1784), 2.0 (mass production, electricity, 1870), 3.0 (automation, computers and electronics, 1969), 4.0 (cyber-physical systems, internet of things, networks, 2011) and 5.0 (today).

Emerging technologies – concerns in the past

Photos of once-new technologies that also raised fears when they appeared: the steam locomotive, the telephone, video tapes, the photo camera and the automobile.

Involved scientific and engineering fields

  • Mechanical engineering: range, load, durability, ability, fluid dynamics
  • Design engineering: visual aspects of the robot
  • Electrical engineering: power, sensing, actuation, electronics
  • Computer science: AI, algorithms, programming, data acquisition and processing
  • Mathematics: control systems
  • Material science: skin, sensors, actuators

Important terminologies

  • Workpiece
  • End effector
  • Payload
  • Degrees of freedom
  • Joints
  • Links
  • Object/body

An industrial arm with its coordinate systems: world coordinate system, robot coordinate system at the base, tool coordinate system at the end effector, and workpiece coordinate system.

Intuition: the terms on one picture

Follow the arm from the floor up. Rigid parts are links; the movable connections between them are joints. The tool at the tip — gripper, welding torch, drill — is the end effector, and the object it works on is the workpiece. The payload is the maximum load the arm can carry at the end effector (manufacturers usually count the gripper's own weight in it). The degrees of freedom count how many independent ways the robot can move.

Degrees of freedom

Two questions on the slide:

  • The robot shown below has a fixed base and four hinge joints. How many DoF of motion does the end effector have? How many DoF does the robot have?
  • How many degrees of freedom does the robot shown below have? (A four-wheeled ground robot on grass.)

An arm with a fixed base and four hinge (revolute) joints, the base frame drawn with X, Y, Z.

What are the answers? (try first)
  • The arm: each hinge joint adds one independent motion, so the robot has 4 DoF — one joint angle per joint. Its end effector can therefore have at most 4 DoF of motion. A free rigid body in space has 6 (3 for position, 3 for orientation), so this arm can't reach every position with every orientation; that needs at least 6 joints.
  • The ground robot: on a flat floor it can move forward/backward, sideways (in principle) and turn about the vertical axis: 3 DoF (x, y, heading). It can't fly up, tilt or roll on purpose. Whether a car-like vehicle can move sideways directly is a different question (it can't, it must manoeuvre), but it can still reach every (x, y, \text{heading}).
Common mistake: "DoF = number of motors" or "more DoF than 6 in space"

DoF counts independent motions, not motors. Two motors driving the same joint add no freedom. And a rigid body in 3D space never has more than 6 DoF of its own (3 translations + 3 rotations). A robot arm can have more than 6 joints (a "redundant" arm, like the human arm), but its end effector still has at most 6 DoF; the extra joints give alternative ways to reach the same pose.

Important terminologies (continued)

  • Coordinate systems
  • Position
  • Orientation (R, P, W)
  • Horizontal reach
  • Vertical reach
  • Work envelope
  • Kinematics

The slide repeats the coordinate-system picture and draws yaw, pitch and roll as rotations about the three axes.

Intuition: position, orientation and reach

Position says where the tool is (x, y, z); orientation says which way it points, given by three angles — roll, pitch and yaw (the slide's "R, P, W"). Together they are the tool's pose. Horizontal and vertical reach are how far out and how high the arm can get, and the work envelope (workspace) is the set of all points it can reach. Kinematics is the maths connecting joint angles to pose — the topic of 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics.

Types of joints

  • Translational motion joints:

    • Linear joint — the output link slides along the input link's axis.
    • Orthogonal joint — the output link slides, at right angles to the input link.

  • Rotary motion joints:

    • Rotational joint — rotation about an axis perpendicular to both links.
    • Twisting joint — rotation about the axis of the links themselves.
    • Revolving joint — the output link, perpendicular to the input link, revolves around the input link's axis.

Each joint is drawn as an input link, an output link and the arrow of the joint motion.

Intuition: two families, five members

Every joint either slides (translational, also called prismatic: a drawer) or turns (rotary, also called revolute: a door hinge). The five names only distinguish how the axis of motion sits relative to the two links. Each such joint adds one degree of freedom. The robot configurations below are named after which kinds of joints they combine.

Structural configurations of industrial robots

Cartesian

(a) Arm configuration with three linear axes x, y, z; (b) its workspace, a rectangular box.

  • Needs a large volume to operate.
  • Has a rigid structure and provides accurate positioning of the end effector.
  • Maintenance is difficult because linear motion is generally obtained by transforming rotary motion.

Cartesian robot:

  • Also called linear robots or gantry robots.
  • They move in straight lines on 3 axes.
  • Simple and easy to program.
  • Have a higher payload carrying capacity.

Pictured: a gantry robot and a 3D printer, which is a small Cartesian robot. The slide also shows a ball screw and a rack and pinion, the parts that turn a motor's rotation into straight motion.

Cylindrical

(a) Arm configuration: rotation \theta about the vertical axis, vertical slide y, horizontal slide z; (b) workspace: a thick-walled cylinder.

  • The arm has one revolute joint and two linear joints.
  • A cylindrical robot might have difficulties touching the floor near its base.
  • Successfully used when the task requires reaching into small openings or working on cylindrical surfaces.

Spherical / polar

(a) Arm configuration: rotations \theta and \phi, extension z; (b) workspace: part of a spherical shell.

  • Large work volume.
  • Can reach all around.
  • Short vertical reach.

Articulated

(a) Arm configuration with only rotary joints (\theta, \phi, \psi); (b) its workspace, a complex rounded volume.

Articulated arm robot:

  • Structure closely resembles the human arm.
  • Can generally achieve its position and orientation in multiple ways.
  • Electrically/hydraulically actuated.
  • 5–6 degrees of freedom.
  • Needs calibration.

Source of the configuration drawings: Introduction to Robotics, S. K. Saha.

Why does each configuration have the workspace shape it has?

Each joint type sweeps out a simple shape, and the workspace is what you get by combining them:

  • Cartesian (3 slides): each slide covers an interval, so the workspace is a box.
  • Cylindrical (1 rotation + 2 slides): turn around the vertical axis × height × radius gives a cylinder — hollow in the middle, because the horizontal slide has a minimum length. That inner hole is why it can't reach near its own base.
  • Spherical (2 rotations + 1 slide): two angles + a distance are exactly spherical coordinates, giving a spherical shell.
  • Articulated (rotations only): link lengths are fixed, so the reachable region is bounded by arcs: a rounded, irregular volume.
Worked example: choosing a configuration from the requirements

Task: a machine must place components with high accuracy across a flat 2\,\mathrm{m} \times 1\,\mathrm{m} table, with plenty of room around it.

  • List the demands: straight-line moves over a rectangular area, high accuracy, simple programming.
  • Match them to the slides: Cartesian robots move in straight lines, have a rigid structure with accurate positioning, and are simple to program; their downside (needing a large volume) is acceptable here.
  • Rule out the others: an articulated arm can do it but is overkill and needs calibration; a cylindrical robot's workspace doesn't match a rectangle.

Choice: a Cartesian (gantry) robot. The method — list the demands, then match them to each configuration's listed strengths and weaknesses — is how the exam's "which robot is suitable, justify" questions are answered (11 Exam Preparation).

Common mistake: "articulated is always best"

Articulated arms are the most flexible, so they look like the universal answer. But flexibility costs: they need calibration, their accuracy and stiffness are usually lower than a gantry's, and programming straight-line moves requires coordinating all joints at once. For a rectangular area or very heavy loads, a Cartesian robot is often better; for fast pick-and-place, a SCARA or delta robot.

End effectors

Grippers

  • Grippers are end effectors used for holding/grasping an object.
  • Used to pick an object and move it to a different position and orientation within the workspace.
  • Applications: pick and place, machine loading, sorting and arranging, material handling etc.
  • Types: mechanical, pneumatic, magnetic, adhesive, hooks and scoops, expandable bladder type.

Pictured: electric, pneumatic, adhesive and magnetic grippers; a suction gripper, a hook and a scoop.

Intuition: matching a gripper to the object

The gripping principle follows from the object's properties. Mechanical/pneumatic fingers clamp most rigid parts. Magnetic grippers only hold ferromagnetic metal (steel sheets). Suction (vacuum) needs a smooth, closed surface (glass, boxes, sheets). Adhesive grippers hold light, delicate or flat objects without pressure. Hooks and scoops carry loads or loose material (sand, soil) instead of grasping.

Jamming of granular material

A video: a gripper made of a balloon filled with granular material wraps around a glass and pours water. When air is sucked out, the grains jam together and the soft balloon turns rigid, holding objects of almost any shape.

Tools

Other end effectors are tools rather than grippers: a welding torch, a drill, a paint sprayer.

SCARA – Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm

A SCARA arm: rotations \theta_1, \theta_2 and \theta_3 about vertical axes, and a vertical linear motion d_4 of the tool.

  • Small size
  • High speed
  • High precision
  • 4 degrees of freedom
  • Applications: assembly, pick and place, PCB soldering, laser engraving
What does "selective compliance" mean?

All of a SCARA's rotation axes are vertical. So the arm is compliant (slightly yielding) sideways, in the horizontal plane, but very stiff vertically. That's exactly what assembly needs: when pushing a peg into a hole, the arm can give a little sideways to centre itself, while the downward push stays firm. Its 4 DoF are x, y, z and rotation about the vertical axis — enough for parts that are put in from above.

Delta robots

  • Delta robots possess three arms connected to a single base, which is mounted above the workspace.
  • The use of parallelograms in the arms maintains the orientation of the end effector.
  • All movement comes from the extremely light robot arms, allowing for low inertia for incredibly fast operating speeds and accelerations.
  • Used in applications requiring high speed and high acceleration.

A video shows the milliDelta (Harvard Wyss Institute), a millimetre-scale delta robot.

Why are delta robots so fast?

The heavy motors sit on the fixed base above the workspace and don't move. Only light rods and the small end-effector platform are accelerated. Less moving mass means lower inertia, so the same motors produce much higher accelerations (Newton's F = ma). The three arms work in parallel, all holding the platform at once, which also keeps it stiff. The price is a small, dome-shaped workspace and small payloads.

Wheeled robots

  • Wheeled robots are robots that navigate around the ground using motorized wheels to propel themselves.
  • They are easier to design, build, and program for movement in flat, not-so-rugged terrain.
  • Robots can have any number of wheels, but three wheels are sufficient for static and dynamic balance.

Number of wheels

One-wheeled robot (Murata Girl): these robots are highly unstable and require extreme engineering and design techniques.

Two-wheeled robots (nBot):

  • Harder to balance than other types, because they must keep moving to stay upright.
  • Usually the center of gravity of these robots is kept below the wheel axle, and the wheels are attached parallel to each other.
  • A tilt sensor is used to determine the tilt angle, and wheel encoders keep track of the position of the platform of the robot.

Three-wheeled robot:

  • They are statically and dynamically stable.
  • The wheels are normally arranged in a triangular manner.
  • Types: differentially steered; single turning wheel.
  • The center of gravity has to lie inside the triangle formed by the wheels.

Four-wheeled robot:

  • Most popular and highly stable.
  • Types: Ackermann steering, differential drive, tank-like steering.

Sketches show which wheels have motors and which are free-turning wheels in each layout.

Why is the centre of gravity inside the wheel triangle the condition for stability?

A robot standing still tips over when the line straight down from its centre of gravity leaves its support area — the polygon spanned by the wheel contact points. Three points always form a triangle, a real area, so a three-wheeled robot can stand with its centre of gravity inside it. With one or two wheels the support "area" is just a point or a line, which is why those robots must balance actively, with sensors and motion.

Connection

Differential drive steers by turning the left and right wheels at different speeds: equal speeds drive straight, opposite speeds turn on the spot. The wheel encoders mentioned for the two-wheeled robot are the position sensors of 2 Sensors.

Types of wheels

  • Cylindrical wheel
  • Omnidirectional wheel with rollers
  • Mecanum wheels

Omnidirectional wheels have small free rollers around the rim, at right angles to the wheel; mecanum wheels have rollers at 45°. The slides show how three omni wheels in a triangle, or four mecanum wheels, combine their motions to drive forwards, sideways, diagonally or to turn on the spot.

Intuition: how a mecanum robot drives sideways

Each mecanum wheel pushes the robot diagonally, because its rollers sit at 45°. Spin all four wheels the same way and the sideways parts cancel: the robot drives straight. Spin the front-left and rear-right wheels one way and the other two the opposite way, and now the forward parts cancel while the sideways parts add up: the robot slides sideways without turning. That's why such robots can reach every (x, y, \text{heading}) directly, without manoeuvring.

Perseverance rover

Not in the 26W slides any more (dropped on 5 Oct 2026); kept here for reference.

Length3 meters
Width2.7 meters
Height2.2 meters
Weight1025 kg

NASA's Mars 2020 rover: 23 cameras in total (9 engineering, 7 science, 7 for entry, descent and landing).

Instruments:

  • Mastcam-Z: an advanced camera system to help study surface minerals.
  • MEDA: a Spanish-built sensor suite to measure temperature, wind speed and direction, pressure, humidity and dust.
  • MOXIE: experiment to demonstrate how astronauts might produce oxygen from Martian CO₂ for breathing and fuel.
  • PIXL: has an X-ray spectrometer to identify chemical elements, and a camera that takes close-up images of rock and soil textures.
  • RIMFAX: a Norwegian-built ground-penetrating radar that will map geology beneath the surface at centimetre scales.
  • SHERLOC: will use spectrometers, a laser and a camera to hunt for organics and minerals that were altered by water.
  • SuperCam: will examine rock and soil with a camera, laser and spectrometers to look for organic compounds.

Aerial robots

Types: air balloon robots, fixed-wing robots, rotary-wing robots, flapping-wing robots.

Aerial robot components:

  • Frame — the X- or +-shaped arms and body of the drone that hold all the parts and pieces together.
  • Motors — the mechanisms that provide power to spin the propellers.
  • ESC (Electronic Speed Control) — connects the battery with the motors, sending signals to each motor to dictate propeller speed.
  • Flight control computer — the brains of the drone, turning electrical signals from the controller into actionable information by sending signals to the ESCs.
  • Telecommunication system.
  • Navigational sensors.
  • Propellers — the spinning blades attached at the end of each arm to achieve lift and direct the motion of the drone.
  • Battery — may be charged in place or in a separate charger, depending on the drone model.
  • Gimbal — a stabilization platform for mounting sensors/instruments.
How does a quadcopter steer with fixed propellers?

It changes the speed of individual motors (through the ESCs). All four faster → climb. Rear pair faster than front → tilt forward and fly forward. Neighbouring propellers spin in opposite directions so their twisting effects cancel; speeding up one diagonal pair and slowing the other makes the drone turn about its vertical axis. The flight computer makes these corrections hundreds of times per second, using the navigation sensors.

Aquatic robots

Robotic boats, submarine robots, underwater crawlers.

Bio-inspired robots

Examples include the Festo elephant trunk (a soft robotic arm), robots modelled on legged animals, snakes, fish and birds.

Humanoid robots

New in the 26W slides.

  • Humanoids: general-purpose, bipedal robots modelled on the human form, designed to work alongside humans to augment productivity.
  • They are characterised by an anthropomorphic design: a torso, a head, two arms and two legs.
  • Some humanoids have only a subset of these body parts.
  • Android: a humanoid robot designed to closely resemble the human physique.
  • Gynoid: sometimes used for robots with a feminine appearance.

Examples pictured: Unitree G1, Boston Dynamics Atlas, Tesla Optimus (image source: humanoid.guide).

Review questions

The last slide shows pictures to discuss: a gantry robot over a greenhouse, a parallel robot, a SCARA kinematic drawing and a small wheeled robot.
